bibliography.note: J. Exp. Biol. 169: 165–179 (1992), issue 1 in Crossref (the entry omits the issue; optional to add). Title and authors match.

claims.claim: pike larvae's mass-specific routine oxygen uptake is independent of mass below about 10 mg
claims.location: p. 165 (PDF p. 1), Summary; p. 170 (PDF p. 6), 'Scaling of physiological rates'
claims.quote: until the larvae had reached a wet body mass of about 10 mg
claims.conditions: laboratory, 15 °C, feeding respirometer, 4-day experiments; wet mass; pike and whitefish (Coregonus lavaretus) alike, from a hatching mass of 1.5–2 mg; above 10 mg pike R_rout = 38.0·m^−0.154 µmol O2 g⁻¹ h⁻¹ (m in mg wet; N = 22, r = 0.93)
claims.note: read in full: the paper's '(…, abstract)' can be dropped.

claims.claim: below 10 g, with Cmax ∝ W^−0.24 (Wieser et al. 1992), … an unfitted 1.25-cm larva at full ration grows 0.23–0.98 mm/day
claims.source_value: −0.24 is the mass exponent of the mass-specific GROWTH rate of pike fed ad libitum, g = 12.0·m^−0.24 (g in mg g⁻¹ h⁻¹, m in mg wet mass; N = 22, r = 0.90), at 15 °C over about 8–1,600 mg wet mass; the paper gives no exponent for consumption or Cmax
claims.location: p. 170 (PDF p. 6), eq. 5; p. 169 (PDF p. 5), Table 1 (mass ranges)
claims.quote: The specific rates of growth also scaled negatively with body mass
claims.conditions: laboratory, 15 °C; pike fed Artemia nauplii (8–50 mg wet, 11 experiments) or roach larvae (200–1,600 mg, 11 experiments); 4-day feeding-respirometer runs
claims.note: using the growth exponent as the Cmax exponent is the project's inference (esocid_larval_energetics.md says 'Wieser's larval growth exponent is −0.24'), and the data stop at 1.6 g (3.6 g counting Wieser & Medgyesy 1991's group E, which is not in eq. 5), not 10 g. Suggested wording: 'with a Cmax mass exponent of −0.24, taken from the mass scaling of the specific growth rate of ad-lib-fed young pike (8–1,600 mg, 15 °C; Wieser et al. 1992)'. Table 1's own ad-lib consumption rates (66.7 J g⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 8–50 mg and 22.1 at 200–1,600 mg per g wet mass; 521 and 143 per g dry mass in Table 2; prey types differ) would imply a steeper consumption slope, about −0.33 wet or −0.39 dry (reader's arithmetic on the ranges' geometric midpoints, ~20 and ~570 mg; rough).

claims.claim: the young pickerel's set: CB −0.24 below 10 g, 'the larval mass exponent (Wieser et al. 1992)'
claims.source_value: −0.24 is the specific growth-rate exponent of ad-lib-fed pike of 8–1,600 mg wet mass at 15 °C, not a consumption exponent
claims.quote: The specific rates of growth also scaled negatively with body mass
claims.note: the src string should say 'growth-rate mass exponent of young pike (Wieser et al. 1992) used as the Cmax exponent'; the 10-g pivot (CA scaled by 10^(CB + 0.24)) extends it beyond the data.

notes: Other values the rewrite may want (all 15 °C, laboratory, wet mass unless stated): growth took 62 ± 3.7 % of metabolizable energy and metabolism 38 % across five groups (Table 2; pike 62–67 %); the yield ratio was ~0.043 mg dry mass per µmol O2; the two smallest pike larvae (8.7 mg wet; 1.01 mg dry) grew 22–24 % a day, and pike routine O2 may reach an aerobic maximum near 200–220 µmol O2 g⁻¹ dry mass h⁻¹ (based on two 4-day experiments only); pike R_max/R_min was 2.4–3.1 versus 1.9–2.1 in whitefish; the Q10 values of whitefish larvae (10 vs 15 °C) were 1.6–2.7. Pike body water was 87.2 % at 8–50 mg and 84.5 % at 200–1,600 mg (Table 1, read on the page image). The esocid_larval_energetics.md note marks this source '[abstract; full text blocked]'; the full text is now in hand and supports its numbers (−0.154 above 10 mg; −0.24 growth; 62 %; 200–220 µmol).
